Acute Kidney Injury in a Child

the labs assign the compartment · prerenal pattern · ibuprofen with volume loss · sediment · fluids, stop the drugIs the kidney still concentrating, and what does the sediment show?

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Assign the compartment from the labs before blaming the drug: BUN:creatinine over 20:1, specific gravity over 1.020 and a bland sediment are prerenal
  • Vomiting or diarrhea on ibuprofen with a prerenal pattern isotonic fluids and stop the NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug); a falling creatinine confirms it
  • Bloody diarrhea days before, then schistocytes and low platelets hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS): supportive care, no antibiotics
What it is

Acute kidney injury (AKI): a rise in creatinine, a fall in urine output, or both, from a prerenal, intrarenal or postrenal cause

Driver

Prerenal: low renal blood flow, tubules intact; intrarenal: tubular necrosis, interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis or HUS; postrenal: obstruction of both outflows

Triggers

Volume loss from vomiting and diarrhea, or diabetic ketoacidosis

An NSAID during volume loss, worse with an ACE inhibitor

Shiga toxin E. coli O157:H7 from undercooked beef, under age 5

Nephrotoxins: aminoglycosides, contrast, heme pigment from rhabdomyolysis

Drug hypersensitivity: NSAIDs after weeks, beta-lactams, proton pump inhibitors

Chain

Volume loss GFR leans on prostaglandins an NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole GFR falls

Prolonged hypoperfusion tubular necrosis: oliguric maintenance with high potassium polyuric recovery with low potassium

Insights

Intact tubules still concentrate: a high specific gravity and urine sodium under 20 mean prerenal, not tubular, injury

Ibuprofen in volume loss acts on blood flow, not by allergy: interstitial nephritis needs days to weeks of the drug and white cells in the urine IbuprofenProstaglandins normally dilate the afferent arteriole; NSAIDs block them, so the afferent arteriole constricts and GFR (glomerular filtration rate) falls. An ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor added on top loosens the efferent side as well.

2Urgent risks
High potassiumHyperkalemia with ECG (electrocardiogram) changes

If the ECG has changed, choose IV calcium to stabilize the heart, then insulin with glucose.

HUSBloody diarrhea 5 to 10 days ago; now pallor, petechiae, oliguria

If the smear shows schistocytes, choose supportive care, dialysis if needed; no antibiotics.

Refractory failureAcidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, volume overload or uremia beyond medical control

If medical treatment fails, choose dialysis (AEIOU).

3Differential
Acute kidney injury: the compartment, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Prerenal (NSAID and volume loss) (prerenal azotemia)Vomiting or diarrhea; an NSAIDBUN:creatinine over 20:1, specific gravity over 1.020, bland sediment; FENa under 1%
Acute interstitial nephritis Which drugsDrugs behind acute interstitial nephritis: DRAINS, for diuretics, rifampin, antibiotics and allopurinol, inhibitors of the proton pump, NSAIDs and sulfa drugs.Drug hypersensitivity: fever, rash, flank painWhite cell casts, sterile pyuria with eosinophils
Acute tubular necrosisIschemia after shock, or a toxin (aminoglycoside, contrast); the commonest intrarenal causeMuddy brown casts; specific gravity about 1.010; FENa over 2%
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
Under 5; bloody diarrhea 5 to 10 days before; E. coli O157:H7Schistocytes, low platelets, hematuria or proteinuria
Immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Poststreptococcal (postinfectious glomerulonephritis): weeks, not days, after strep, about 1 to 3 weeks after the throat and up to about 6 after impetigo; IgA nephropathy (Berger disease): gross hematuria during an upper respiratory infectionHematuria and proteinuria, red cell casts; low C3 in poststreptococcal
Postrenal obstruction
Obstruction of both kidneys' outflow, or of a solitary kidneyRenal US or a postvoid residual
Rhabdomyolysis
Muscle injury or a seizure; heme pigment injures the tubulesDipstick blood with few red cells on microscopy
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Specific gravity about 1.010 after shockTubules can no longer concentrateSupportive care; watch potassium
Polyuria days into tubular necrosisRecovery phaseWatch for low potassium
An NSAID added to an ACE inhibitorBoth arterioles lose their toneStop the NSAID and give fluids

Pause point. The bait: furosemide or a renal US for a prerenal pattern. Intact tubules need volume: isotonic fluids and stopping the ibuprofen.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining patterns Prerenal – BUN:creatinine over 20:1, specific gravity over 1.020, bland sediment, FENa under 1%, urine sodium under 20 · Acute tubular necrosis – muddy brown casts, specific gravity about 1.010, BUN:creatinine under 15, FENa over 2%, urine sodium over 40 · Postrenal – obstruction of both outflows; early, FENa under 1% and BUN:creatinine over 15, like prerenal; long-standing, FENa over 2%, BUN:creatinine under 15, urine sodium over 40

7Treatment
1

Prerenalvolume loss with a prerenal pattern

IV (intravenous) isotonic fluid bolus; stop the NSAID
2

Intrarenalthe cause is in the kidney

Interstitial nephritis: stop the drug; tubular necrosis and HUS: supportive care

HUS from E. coli usually remits with supportive care; no antibiotics.

3

Potassiumhyperkalemia with ECG changes

IV calcium, then insulin with glucose
4

Dialysisan AEIOU trigger despite treatment

Hemodialysis or hemofiltration

Over half of children with HUS need it.

8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
After isotonic fluidsA falling creatinine confirms prerenal injury
Tubular necrosis, maintenance phaseOliguria: watch for high potassium and uremia
Tubular necrosis, recovery phasePolyuria: watch for low potassium and electrolyte wasting
Practice
  1. 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea on ibuprofen, BUN/Cr 32:1, SG 1.028, bland urinalysis → Isotonic fluids and stop the ibuprofen
  2. 5 yo F, bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pallor, petechiae, oliguria, schistocytes on smear → Hemolytic uremic syndrome → supportive care; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents
  3. 68 yo F on naproxen for 3 weeks, fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts → Acute interstitial nephritis → stop the NSAID
  4. 60 yo M after septic hypotension, SG 1.010, muddy brown granular casts, BUN/Cr 14:1 → Ischemic acute tubular necrosis
  5. 74 yo M on lisinopril and furosemide who starts ibuprofen, creatinine rising from 1.1 to 2.0 → Discontinue the ibuprofen and give fluids → the "triple whammy" of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID
  6. 16 yo M, gross hematuria 2 days into a URI, normal C3 → IgA nephropathy → timing with the URI and normal complement decide
  7. 7 yo M, cola-colored urine and periorbital edema 2 weeks after pharyngitis, low C3 → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → supportive care
Pearls Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor drop GFR (glomerular filtration rate) from opposite ends. An NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin II receptor blocker) plus a diuretic is the "triple whammy" · FENa (fractional excretion of sodium) <1% supports prerenal but is unreliable after diuretics · the AIN (acute interstitial nephritis) triad is present in a minority; WBC (white blood cell) casts carry the diagnosis · PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) vs IgA nephropathy is timing plus complement. PSGN comes weeks, not days, after the infection (about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 after impetigo) with low C3; IgA nephropathy comes during the URI (upper respiratory infection) with normal C3.
Pairs with Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers sorting by smear and coagulation studies when renal failure comes with a falling platelet count.
Transferable rule Read the ratio, then the specific gravity, then the sediment, and only then the drug. When a full chemistry panel is given, read it before answering.
Salient decoyDrug-induced interstitial nephritis: the named drug draws attention to it, but the timeline and the sediment are wrong.
True-fact-wrong-slotHUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): gastroenteritis cues it, but it needs bloody diarrhea, schistocytes and an active sediment.
